lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Opening admiration for her verses; establishes the literary courtship.

lines.text: Such a letter from such a hand!
lines.note: Her awed response to his letter; shows the first spark.

lines.text: And in the meantime I have learnt to know your voice, not merely from the poetry but from the kindness in it.
lines.note: She hears his kindness in his voice, not only his poetry.

lines.text: See now, how, of that 'Friendship' you offer me (and here Juliet's word rises to my lips)--I feel sure once and for ever.
lines.note: He answers her offered friendship with certainty.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Her playful redefinition of spring; a private stylistic joke.

lines.text: I do not find it take away from my feeling of the magnanimity of Prometheus that he should, in truth, complain (as he does from beginning to end) of what he finds himself suffering.
lines.note: His reading of Prometheus; early shared Greek ground.

lines.text: Oh! the 'Flight of the Duchess'--do let us hear more of her!
lines.note: Her delight in the Duchess; a poem that becomes theirs.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: He frames love beyond any possible loss.

lines.text: And now I will dare ... yes, dearest, kiss you back to my heart again; my own.
lines.note: A tender promise to kiss her back to his heart.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: She calls his love a dream made real.

lines.text: 'Luria' is to climb to the place of a great work, I see.
lines.note: She sees Luria growing into a great work.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: He jokes that marriage would have to be invented.
She says you are her one light.
